34-014.r: Main source of Mughal state income → land revenue, taken from the peasant's surplus produce.

34-015.r: 'Maal' in Mughal administrative vocabulary → land revenue.

34-016.r: Tobacco (brought by the Portuguese) → banned by Jahangir in 1617 A.D. for its harmful effects.

34-017.r: Madad-i-Maash → revenue-free land grants to learned, pious or worthy persons, saints and religious institutions, as charity.

34-018.r: Chakla → Mughal territorial unit between Subah and Pargana, but not the same as Sarkar; used especially under Shah Jahan.

34-020.r: Mansabdari existed under the Mughals; mansabdars were appointed by the King on qualification; both true, R not the explanation.

34-021.r: Mansabdari covered both military and civil posts, so both statements true; Abul Fazl lists 66 grades, but only 33 were in practice.

34-022.r: Diwan-i-Tan → jagirs and salaries; Mustarfi → audit of state income-expenditure; Mushrif → office; Vakianvis → record of main events and firmans.

34-023.r: Diwans → Akbar: Muzaffar Khan; Jahangir: Ghiyas Beg Itmadud-Daulah; Shah Jahan: Sadullah Khan; Aurangzeb: Asad Khan.

34-024.r: Akbar regulated currency like Sher Shah (gold coins, silver rupees, copper Dams); Dam was the chief copper coin; both true, R not the explanation.

34-025.r: Coins with Rama and Sita figures and Devanagari legend 'Ram Siya' → issued by Akbar.

34-026.r: Mughal coins → gold Mohur, silver Rupee, copper Dam (Daam).

34-027.r: Silver coin 'Shahrukh' → introduced by Babur, along with copper coins.

34-028.r: Mughal coin terms → Khazana: minted in earlier reigns; Chalani: current reign's coins; Taza sikka: newly minted this or last year.

34-029.r: Batai (Bantai) → crop sharing of real produce between state and peasant; Sher Shah's methods: Nasq/Muktai/Kankut, Nakadi or Jabti, Galla Bakshi or Bantai.

34-030.r: Deccan land revenue under Akbar → paid per plough (number of ploughs); Todarmal's systematic method existed only in North India (J.N. Sarkar).

34-031.r: Shahab (Shihab) Canal → Akbar-era restoration of Firuz Shah's Rajabwah by Delhi governor Shihabuddin Khan, for irrigation.

35-001.r: Mughal paintings → battle scenes, animals, birds, nature and courtiers (all); a blend of Indian, Persian and Islamic styles.

35-002.r: Foundation of Mughal painting → Humayun, during exile in Persia and Afghanistan, with painters Khwaja Abdus Samad and Mir Sayyid Ali.

35-003.r: Painting Karkhana (Tasvir Khana) → set up by Akbar: Agra (1558-1572), Fatehpur Sikri (1572-1585), Lahore (1585-1601), Agra again (1603-1605).

35-004.r: Mughal painting shaped the Pahari, Rajasthani and Kangra styles; Kalighata (Kalighat) painting was indigenous and not affected.

35-005.r: Dastan-i-Amir Hamza → earliest Mughal illustrated manuscript, begun under Humayun; took 15 years, about 100 artists, under Mir Sayyid Ali and Abdus Samad.
35-005.c: Book prints two answers, (a) Abdus Samad and (c) Mir Sayyid Ali.

35-006.r: Daswant and Basawan → painters of Akbar's court; Ain-i-Akbari lists them with Keshav Lal, Mukund, Mishkin, Farrukh.

35-007.r: European painting → reached Akbar's court through the Portuguese; taught portraits and drawing distant objects smaller.

35-008.r: Jahangir's painters → Abul Hasan and Aqa Riza (also Mansur, Bishan Das, Manohar, Govardhan); Abdus Samad and Mir Sayyid Ali belong to Humayun's time.

35-009.r: Not Jahangir's painter → Khwaja Abdus Samad (Humayun and Akbar); Mansur, Manohar and Abul Hasan were Jahangir's (1605-27).

35-010.r: Mughal painting flourished under Jahangir (1605-27): he had his own atelier and loved portraiture; painting was the art he chiefly patronised.

35-012.r: Shift from illustrated manuscripts to albums and portraits → Jahangir; favoured scenes of his own life, portraits, birds, flowers, animals.

35-013.r: Pahari, Rajput, Mughal and Kangra Schools → styles of painting; Pahari = painting of hill states of the north-western Himalaya.

35-014.r: Kishangarh School (Rajasthan) → painting; famous for Bani Thani; inspired by Sawant Singh (throne 1748), Radha-Krishna theme.

35-015.r: Aurangzeb banned music yet played the Veena; many Persian books on Indian classical music were written in his reign.

35-016.r: Raga sung early in the morning → Todi (Hindustani classical).

35-017.r: Swami Haridas (guru of Tansen, Baiju Bawra, Gopal Nayak; Dhrupad) → followers set up 5 centres: Banke Bihariji, Nidhivan, Gorelal temple, Rasik Bihari, Thatti Khana.

35-018.r: Not correct: title 'Tansen' came from Raja Vikramjit Singh of Gwalior, not Akbar; Akbar gave 'Mian'; early patron Raja Ramchandra Singh of Rewa.

35-019.r: Dhrupad singers of Akbar's reign → Tansen and Swami Haridas; Vilas Khan was the main singer under Jahangir.

35-020.r: Tansen's tomb → Gwalior, near Saint Hazrat Ghaus's tomb; first patron Raja Ramchandra of Rewa (Bhata), then Akbar (one of nine jewels).

35-022.r: Tansen's original name → Ramtanu Pandey; one of Akbar's Navaratnas; Akbar's titles 'Miyan' and 'Kanthabharanvanivilas'.

35-023.r: Mal Gurjari → a Raga invented by Raja Mansingh Tomar, not a person; Mansingh Tomar, Tansen, Sadarang–Adarang were greats of Hindustani music.

35-024.r: Akbar → learnt Hindu music from Lala Kalawant.

35-025.r: Tappa style → refined at Muhammad Shah's court (18th century); based on folk songs of Punjab's camel drivers; Sadarang-Adarang composed Khayal there.

36-001.r: Baburnama into English → John Leyden and William Erskine.

36-002.r: Gulbadan Begum (1523-1603) → daughter of Babur; wrote 'Humayun Nama' on Akbar's orders, a history of Babur and Humayun.

36-006.r: Khairul Manzil mosque (opposite Purana Qila, Delhi; later 'Madarsa-e-Begum') → built by Maham Anaga.

36-008.r: Hitopadesha into Persian → Taj-ul-Din Mufti al-Maliki (Tajul Mali), titled 'Mufarrih-al-Qubal'.

36-009.r: Hasan Nizami → Tazul Maasir; Khwandamir → Humayun Nama; Muhammad Qazim → Alamgir Nama; Bhim Sen → Nushkha-i-Dilkusha.
36-009.t: Khwandamir's Humayun Nama differs from Gulbadan Begum's.

36-010.r: Mulla Daud → Chandayan; Damodar Kavi → Padmavati Katha; Somnath → Rag Vibodh; Amir Khusro → Ashiqa.

36-011.r: Alamgir Nama → Munshi Mohd. Qazim; Tabaqat-i-Akbari → Nizamuddin Ahmad; Chahar Chaman → Chandrabhan Barahman; Iqbal Nama-Jahangiri → Muitamad Khan.

36-013.r: Tabaqat-i-Akbari (sometimes more reliable than Akbarnama) → Nizamuddin Ahmad; Humayun-Nama → Gulbadan Begum; Padshahnama → Abdul Hamid Lahori.

36-014.r: Greatest Muslim contributor to Hindi literature → Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khana ('Rahim Satsai'), master of Arabic, Persian, Turkish, Sanskrit, Hindi, Rajasthani.

36-015.r: Abdul Hamid Lahori → official historian of Shah Jahan's reign; wrote 'Padshahnama' (Badshahnama).

36-016.r: Shahjahannama (17th century) → Inayat Khan; translated into English by A.R. Fuller (19th century).

36-017.r: Correct pair → Babur: Tuzuk-i-Baburi (Turkish); Humayun-Nama → Gulbadan Begum; Tarikh-i-Sher Shahi → Abbas Khan Sarwani; Tabaqat-i-Akbari → Nizamuddin Ahmad.

36-018.r: Wrong pair → Tughluqnama is Amir Khusro's; Ibn Battuta wrote 'Rihla'; Tabaqat-i-Nasiri → Minhaj; Tarikh-i-Firuzshahi → Shams-i-Siraj-Afif; Humayun Nama → Gulbadan.

36-019.r: Panchatantra in Persian → 'Anwar-i-Suhaili' (Mulla Husain Waaiz Kashifi), 'Kalila-wa Dimnah' (Nashurullah), 'Ayar-i-Danish' (Abul Fazl).

36-020.r: Yogavasistha into Persian → Nizamuddin Panipati, in Akbar's reign.

36-021.r: Akbarnama → written by Abul Fazl from 1590 to 1596 A.D.; key: seven years (some books say 12 or 13).
36-021.c: UPPSC did not evaluate this question, as sources differ on how long Akbarnama took.

36-022.r: Ain-i-Akbari → by Abul Fazl, Akbar's court historian, in Persian; deals with Akbar's administration.

36-023.r: Akbarnama's three volumes → first: Akbar's ancestors; second: Akbar's reign; third: Ain-i-Akbari (administration, court, army, revenue, geography).

36-024.r: Mughal court language → Persian; Akbar set up a translation department for Sanskrit, Arabic, Turkish and Greek works.

36-025.r: Mughal official and court language → Persian; Urdu was the language of princely courts such as Delhi and Lucknow.
36-025.t: Don't pick Turkish: Babur wrote in it, but the court language was Persian.

36-027.r: Bhimsen Kayestha → Tarikh-i-Dilkusha; Chandrabhan Brahman → Chahar Chaman; Ishwardas Nagar → Futuhat-i-Alamgiri; Sujanrai Bhandari → Khulasat-ut-Tawarikh.

36-028.r: Futuhat-i-Alamgiri → Ishwardas Nagar, a Mughal officer; records events of Aurangzeb's reign.

36-029.r: Nastaliq → Persian script used in medieval (Mughal) India; Aurangzeb was an expert in writing it.

36-030.r: Nagri Das (Servant of Radha) → Raja Sawant Singh of Kishangarh, poet of verses praising Krishna; Kishangarh rulers patronised the Nimbarka sect.

36-031.r: 'Rama Chandrika' and 'Rasik-Priya' → Keshavdas (1555-1617 A.D.), Sanskrit scholar and Hindi poet; Rasik Priya pioneered the Ritikaal.

36-032.r: 'Ramachandrika' → Keshavdas; Ratan Bavani, Rasikpriya and Kavipriya are also his.

36-033.r: Keshavdas → Ramachandrika, Rasik Priya, Ratan Bavani, Kavipriya, Chhandamala; Ram Rasayan, Ganga Lahari, Prabodh Pachasa → Padmakar.
36-033.t: Ram Rasayan is Padmakar's, not Keshavdas's.

37-001.r: Wrong pair → Akbar: Thomas Roe (Roe came 1615 under Jahangir; Akbar died 1605); Jahangir: Hawkins; Shah Jahan: Tavernier; Aurangzeb: Manucci.

37-002.r: Diamonds and diamond mines of India → described by Jean-Baptiste Tavernier (1605-1689), 17th-century French gem merchant and traveller.

37-003.r: Palace of forty pillars at Allahabad (Akbar's time) → William Finch said five to twenty thousand men worked forty years on it.

37-004.r: Travellers → Hawkins 1608-1611; Thomas Roe 1615-1619; Manucci 1653-1708; Ralph Fitch 1583-1586.
37-004.c: Answer not printed; the explanation's pairs fit code (b), though the list gives Fitch 1585-1586.

37-005.r: Chronology → Jahangir (1605-1627) – Muhammad Shah (1719-1748) – Ahmad Shah Abdali (Panipat III, January 14, 1761) – Bahadur Shah II (1837-1857).

37-006.r: Invasions in order → Genghis Khan (Iltutmish's reign) – Timur (1398) – Nadir Shah (1739, Muhammad Shah) – Ahmad Shah Abdali (1748-69).

37-007.r: True: Abdali fought Panipat III (1761); Jahangir loved beauty and nature. False: Aybak, not Babur, founded the Delhi Sultanate; Shah Jahan's sons fought the succession war.

37-008.r: Nadir Shah's Delhi massacre → 1739 (Karnal); Panipat I (Babur–Ibrahim Lodi) → 1526; Panipat II (Hemu–Akbar) → 1556; Panipat III (Abdali–Marathas) → 1761.

37-009.r: Hem Chandra Vikramaditya → Hemu, army chief and Prime Minister of Adil Shah Suri; won 22 battles; took title Vikramaditya after beating Targi Begh.

37-010.r: 'The last Sun of Indian glory' → Prithviraj Chauhan, according to historian B.N. Luniya.

37-011.r: Father → son: Babur → Kamran; Akbar → Salim; Shah Jahan → Murad (Bakhsh); Jahangir → Khusrau.

37-012.r: Wrong pair → Second Battle of Panipat (1556) was Hemu vs Akbar, not Tipu Sultan vs Marathas; Haldighati (18 June 1576) and Panipat I (1526) are correct.

37-013.r: Third Battle of Panipat → 1761; Second Battle of Tarain → 1192; Death of Akbar → 1605; Death of Aurangzeb → 1707.

37-014.r: Haldighati → Akbar (vs Rana Pratap); Bilgram → Humayun (vs Sher Shah); Revolt of Khusrau → Jahangir; Khanwa → Babur (vs Rana Sanga).

37-015.r: 1556 → Accession of Akbar; 1600 → Charter to East India Company; 1680 → Death of Shivaji; 1739 → Nadir Shah captures Delhi.
37-015.t: Haldighati is the extra distractor; it does not fit any of these years.

37-016.r: Years → Third Battle of Panipat 1761; Haldighati 1576; Second Battle of Tarain 1192; Battle of Asirgarh 1601.

37-017.r: Correct pair → Haldighati 1576; Chausa was June 1539, Kanauj May 1540, Khajwa January 1659, Kheda (Shahu vs Tarabai) 1707.

37-018.r: Chronology → Khanwa (1527, Babur vs Rana Sanga) – Ghaghra (1529, Babur vs Mahmud Lodi, his last battle) – Chausa (1539) – Samugarh.

37-019.r: Chronology → Daurah (1532) – Chausa (25/26 June 1539) – Kannauj/Bilgram (May 1540) – Samugarh (29 May 1658).

37-021.r: Wrong pair → Battle of Balkh was in Shah Jahan's reign, not Jahangir's; Babur–Khanwa, Humayun–Chausa and Akbar–Haldighati are correct.

37-022.r: Ata Ali Khan → Tansen's name after converting to Islam (real name Ramtanu Pandey); hence 'None of these'.

37-023.r: Iqta → Delhi Sultans; Jagir → Mughals; Amaram → Vijayanagara; Mokasa → Marathas.

37-024.r: Babul Mecca (Gate of Mecca) → Surat, the Haj pilgrims' port in Mughal times; also called 'Meccai dwar' and 'Meccabari'.

37-026.r: Nawruz festival → adopted by the Mughals from the Zoroastrians of Persia (Iran); celebrated for nineteen days; Badauni called it 'Nawruz-i-Jalali'.

37-027.r: Mughal-era madrasa for Muslim Jurisprudence → Lucknow; Mulla Nizamuddin of Sihali began 'Darse Nizami' (Tafsir, Hadith, Fiqh).

37-028.r: Chronology → Sheikh Mubarak died 1593 – Faizi died 1595 – Abul Fazl murdered 1602 (on Prince Salim's order) – Daniyal died 1605.

37-029.r: Chronology → Padmini (Chittor, Khalji's time) – Durgavati (Gondwana, fought Akbar) – Tara Bai (Rajaram's queen) – Ahilya Bai (Holkar queen of Malwa).

37-030.r: Correct pair → Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khanan's tomb: Delhi; Salim Chishti's tomb: Fatehpur Sikri; Itmad-ud-Daula: Agra; Aurangzeb: Khuldabad.

37-031.r: Both wrong: Buland Darwaza is red sandstone with marble decoration, and marble went into Salim Chishti's tomb, not Khankah; Bara Imambara, Rumi Darwaza used bricks and lime.

37-032.r: Tombs → Babur: Kabul (Afghanistan); Humayun: Delhi; Jahangir: Lahore (Pakistan); Shah Jahan: Agra.

37-033.r: Wrong pair → Jahangiri Mahal is in Agra (built by Akbar), not Burhanpur; Sher Shah's Tomb–Sasaram and Bibi ka Maqbara–Aurangabad are correct.

37-034.r: Chronology → Atala Mosque, Jaunpur (c. 1408) – Sher Shah's Tomb, Sasaram (1540-45) – Humayun's Tomb (1565-72) – Rabia Daurani's Tomb, Aurangabad.

37-035.r: Babur → Jama Masjid (Sambhal); Humayun → Din Panah; Akbar → Jahangiri Mahal; Jahangir → Itmad-ud-Daula's Mausoleum.

37-036.r: Qutb Minar → Iltutmish; Gol Gumbad → Muhammad Adil Shah; Buland Darwaza → Akbar; Moti Masjid (Delhi) → Aurangzeb.

37-038.r: Alai Darwaza → Alauddin Khalji; Buland Darwaza → Akbar; Moti Masjid, Agra → Shah Jahan; Moti Masjid, Delhi → Aurangzeb.

37-039.r: Muallim (Mughal period) → navigator on Indian merchant ships; used a spherical device to read stars and sun for the ship's position.
37-039.c: Answer not printed: no option fits; a Muallim was a ship's employee, not a ship.

37-040.r: Banjaras (medieval India) → traders moving in caravans of oxen with grain, salt and ghee; also skilled in textile embroidery.

37-041.r: Sarais → square or rectangular rest houses giving temporary stay to Indian and foreign travellers, pilgrims, merchants and traders.

37-042.r: Wrong pair: Jarib was a land measuring unit, not a tax; Dam = copper coin (Rupiyah = 40 dam); Desai = Maratha district revenue collector; Diwan = provincial revenue head.

38-001.r: Guru Nanak's successor → Bhai Lehna, later known as Guru Angad; Nanak died September 22, 1539, aged 70.

38-003.r: Successor chosen by Guru Nanak before his death (1539 A.D.) → Guru Angad.

38-004.r: Gurumukhi script ('from the mouth of the Guru') → started by the second Sikh Guru, Guru Angad.

38-005.r: Amritsar → founded by fourth Guru Ramdas on about 500 bighas granted by Akbar; he dug the holy tank; son Guru Arjan completed the temple.

38-007.r: Correct pair → Guru Arjan Dev: Adi Granth (1604); Amardas set up 22 Manjis; Dal Khalsa → Kapur Singh; Arjan was executed by Jahangir for aiding Khusrau.

38-008.r: Guru who sheltered and helped rebel Prince Khusrau (1606) → Guru Arjan Dev, fifth Guru; Jahangir had him executed; he built Harmandir Sahib, Amritsar.

38-009.r: Adi Granth (Guru Granth Sahib) → compiled by fifth Guru Arjan Dev (1581-1606); includes Kabir, Baba Farid, Namdev, Raidas, Jaydev, and Guru Tegh Bahadur.

38-010.r: Sikh Gurus executed → Guru Arjan Dev (by Jahangir, 1606, for helping Khusrau) and Guru Tegh Bahadur (by Aurangzeb, November 1675, Chandni Chowk).
38-010.h: Earlier Guru with earlier emperor: Arjan–Jahangir, then Tegh Bahadur–Aurangzeb.

38-012.r: Famous Sikh Gurudwara → Hem Kund (Chamoli, Uttarakhand).

38-013.r: Born in Patna (1666 A.D.) → Guru Gobind Singh, tenth and last Sikh Guru, founder of the 'Khalsa Panth'.

38-014.r: Nanded (Maharashtra), sacred to Sikhs → Guru Gobind Singh was killed there by an Afghan noble; Takhat Sachkhand Sri Hazur Sahib stands at his cremation site.

38-015.r: Guru Gobind Singh's greatness → formed the Sikh military order 'Khalsa'; surnames Singh/Kaur; 5 K's: Kesh, Kangha, Kachha, Kripan, Kada.

38-017.r: Khalsa Panth → founded 13th April 1699 (Baisakhi) at Anandpur Sahib by tenth Guru Gobind Singh, the last Sikh prophet; over 300 years ago.

38-021.r: Original name of Banda Bahadur → Lachhman Dev (Lachman Dev); linked to Guru Gobind Singh.
